claims.text: The baseline Hf-Mo-Ta-Ti-Zr alloy is a single-phase BCC solid solution.
The asymmetric XRD peaks of the baseline alloy arise from dendritic versus interdendritic compositional micro-segregation.
The baseline Hf-Mo-Ta-Ti-Zr alloy has low room-temperature fracture strain.
Adding approximately 4 at.% Cr to Hf-Mo-Ta-Ti-Zr will induce a multicomponent Laves phase.
The Cr-induced Laves phase may have a stoichiometry such as (Hf,Zr,Ti)2(Mo,Cr).
At approximately 4 at.% Cr, the Laves-phase volume fraction will be approximately 4 vol%.
The Laves phase will nucleate preferentially in interdendritic regions because of micro-segregation.
The Laves phase will form a reticulated or interconnected morphology.
A reticulated Laves-phase network will impede crack extension by deflecting cracks and increasing fracture-surface area.
Cr solute atoms produce local lattice distortion and strain fields in the BCC matrix through atomic-size mismatch with Hf, Zr, and Ta.
Cr-induced lattice distortion will provide solid-solution hardening and increase yield strength.
Cr addition will contract the BCC lattice because Cr has a smaller atomic radius than Hf, Zr, and Ta.
The BCC lattice parameter will decrease by approximately 0.005-0.01 Å after adding Cr.
Annealing in the stated 1000-1200 °C range can enable Laves-phase precipitation.
The Laves-phase fraction and morphology depend on thermal processing, including cooling rate and heat treatment.
The Cr-containing alloy will have greater fracture strain than the baseline when the Laves network is interconnected but does not create a catastrophic continuous brittle path.
Increasing Cr beyond approximately 4 at.% may increase the Laves-phase fraction or make its morphology continuous and embrittling.

HRTEM with EDS mapping can distinguish Cr-specific Laves-phase formation from baseline micro-segregation by testing whether Cr enrichment co-localizes with identified Laves precipitates and is depleted from the BCC matrix.
